Quick Brief

30 days

Time-to-trust roadmap

3-tier

Token architecture (primitive → semantic → component)

Zero

Hard-coded values in stable components

"

The real problem isn't broken components — it's invisible ones. Teams stop using a design system when they can't trust it. My first 30 days are about earning trust through quick, visible fixes, not a six-week audit report nobody reads.

02

The Problem

What a broken design system actually looks like

I've rebuilt a design system from scratch at CYGNVS — cross-platform (Web / iOS / Android). The recurring pattern: systems don't fail because of bad components, they fail because of invisible ones. Hard-coded hex values, raw spacing numbers, no token adoption, documentation nobody reads, and engineers who stopped trusting Figma three sprints ago.

Three failure modes

Failure mode 1

Token adoption gap

Hard-coded hex values, raw spacing numbers, and inline font sizes scattered across components. Figma Analytics reveals the true scale.

Failure mode 2

Invisible broken components

Teams build workarounds rather than flag issues. The system appears stable while quietly diverging from production.

Failure mode 3

Documentation nobody reads

Written for completeness, not for the person searching at 11 PM with a deadline. No clear reader type, no rationale, no ownership.

03

The Approach

First 30 days — earn trust, then scale

Rather than disappearing for a month and re-emerging with "v2," I fix P1 issues in the live library with a clear changelog, open a #design-system Slack channel, and make progress visible weekly.

1

Audit fast (Week 1)

Two parallel tracks:

  • Figma Analytics + codebase scan: how many hard-coded hex values, raw spacing numbers, or inline font sizes exist? This reveals the true "token adoption gap."
  • 20-minute interviews with 3–4 designers and 2 engineers. Question: "What's the one thing in the system that costs you the most time?" Listen for patterns, not feature requests.

Score every issue against two axes: frequency and effort. High-frequency, low-effort issues become Week 3 fixes. Everything else gets sequenced.

Critically: map each issue to its Atomic level — is this broken at the token/atom level, or a molecule/organism that's only broken because its underlying atom is wrong? Fixing a token fixes every component that inherits it.

2

Ship tokens before components (Week 2–3)

Three-tier token architecture:

  • Primitive: color.primitive.B500 = #1773D1
  • Semantic: color.semantic.surface.default → color.primitive.B500
  • Component: color.component.button.bg.primary → color.semantic.surface.default

Output per platform:

// CSS
--ds-button-bg-primary: #1773D1;

// Swift
DSColor.buttonBgPrimary

Verifying developer implementation: visual QA session with Figma frame and live build side-by-side, plus a token audit script that confirms no hard-coded values remain. Run before every component is marked "stable."

3

Fix high-impact components (Week 3–4)

Before "shipped" checklist: token parity, responsive breakpoints, dark mode, keyboard a11y, motion. No exceptions — a component without documentation is "beta," not "stable."

4

Atomic structure as shared mental model

Atomic Design isn't just a filing system — it's a shared mental model. When designers and engineers use the same vocabulary (atoms, molecules, organisms), handoffs shrink, reviews get faster, and contribution guidelines write themselves.

Atomic levelContentsAudit focus
Foundations / AtomsTokens, typography, spacing, icons, single button, input fieldToken consistency
MoleculesSearch bar, form field — simple testable combosComposition
OrganismsNav bar, data table, card gridResponsive behaviour
Templates / PagesDashboards, forms, empty states — usage guidelines onlyHandoff boundary

04

The Result

Documentation strategy

Documentation fails when it's written for completeness, not for the person searching at 11 PM with a deadline. I write for two reader types: the designer asking "when do I use this?" and the engineer asking "how do I build this?"

Doc layer

Foundations

Tokens, typography scale, colour system, spacing, motion principles. The “why” behind every visual decision.

Doc layer

Components (Molecules & Organisms)

Anatomy, states, usage do/don't, props/variants, a11y notes, code snippet. Each page declares its Atomic level and links to consuming organisms.

Doc layer

Patterns (Templates & Pages)

“Use a ghost button when the action is secondary to the primary CTA on the same surface” — not “A ghost button has a transparent background.” Every rule has a rationale.

Dual-tool approach

Notion hosts decision logs, principles, and visual usage guidance — the "why" layer Storybook can't carry.

A Storybook component page links to Notion rationale. A Notion component page links to the live Storybook story.

Quality gates

  • A component without documentation is not "stable" — it's "beta." No exceptions.
  • Quarterly doc review sprint: every component page has a one-click "Flag as outdated" link that creates a Jira ticket.

05

Learning

What I'd do differently

A roadmap is a hypothesis. These are the three calls I'd revisit if I were briefed on a new system tomorrow.

1

Start with engineer pain, not designer pain

The token adoption gap is always wider on the engineering side. I'd run the codebase scan before the designer interviews — it reframes every conversation that follows.

2

Ship a “system health” dashboard on day 1

A visible, auto-updating metric (% token adoption, % components documented) changes the team's relationship with the system. Progress you can see compounds faster than progress you report in a slide deck.

3

Contribution model needs teeth, not guidelines

“Anyone can contribute” doesn't work without a clear review SLA and an owner for each Atomic level. I'd assign molecule/organism ownership in week 1, not week 6.
